case_study_insert.main_stem: Northbridge Learning Group (NLG) is a private limited company in the private education sector, based in the Melbourne area and running tutorial colleges, employing a workforce of 55. Founded in 2015 by Elena Vasquez, it works with local schools and operates a flat structure with laissez-faire leadership. NLG plans to invest $640,000 in a new digital learning studio with tablet-based courses, financed by a $400,000 ten-year bank loan, $200,000 retained profit and a $40,000 overdraft. It has fixed costs of $216,000 a year, a variable cost of $10 a unit and a selling price of $28, and produces 50,000 units a year. NLG faces an online-course content error rate of 4.1% and tutor absenteeism of 9%.
case_study_insert.appendix_1_marketing_ops: Quality and Operations Log — Q4 2025: The studio delivered 11,200 course places last quarter with a content error rate of 4.1%, up from 2.3% a year earlier. Student complaints rose from 22 to 40 a month. Average marker feedback time is 5.6 days. A survey of 400 parents found 72% would pay $20 more for small-group digital tutoring, and 60% check pass rates before enrolling. A skills audit shows 18 of 55 tutors have not completed on-the-job training on the new learning platform; off-the-job training courses at the city college cost $540 per tutor.

appendix_2_financial_data.title: Extract from the Statement of Profit or Loss and Capital employed data of Northbridge Learning Group for the year ended 31 March 2025 ($ '000)

case_study_insert.appendix_3_external_environment: Economic and Education Bulletin (November 2026): (1) The central bank raised the base interest rate from 3.75% to 4.50%, raising borrowing costs for businesses with variable-rate loans. (2) The national minimum wage will rise by 6.2% from $13.80 to $14.66 per hour from April 2026, lifting tutor support payroll costs. (3) Tablet and cloud-licence input costs have risen 8.4% year-on-year, while demand for digital tutoring grew 5.1%.

questions.question_text: NLG is funding part of its $640,000 digital learning studio with a $400,000 ten-year bank loan. Explain two advantages for NLG of using the $200,000 retained profit instead of borrowing more.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Retained profit carries no interest or compulsory repayment, so NLG protects the cash flow needed to meet fixed costs of $216,000 a year while it services the $400,000 loan and the $40,000 overdraft. Every dollar not paid to the bank can absorb the 8.4% rise in tablet and cloud-licence costs, helping NLG hold its $28 selling price and keep the studio attractive to the local schools that refer students.

Point 2: Using $200,000 retained profit keeps Elena Vasquez's ownership intact and avoids more collateral risk. The $640,000 studio cannot be repossessed if enrolments fall short of the 50,000 units target, and the survey showing 72% of 400 parents would pay $20 more for small-group tutoring gives NLG confidence to fund the launch internally rather than increase its bank debt. With a 4.1% content error rate and 9% tutor absence already threatening the 11,200 course places, cash kept inside the business can be redirected to rework and cover without asking the bank; it also avoids lender conditions on studio operations.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid advantage identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for contextual explanation and analysis applied to NLG's financing decision and its college operations.

questions.question_text: NLG is promoting its new tablet-based courses. Consider national television advertising, partnerships with local schools, or social media campaigns. Which should NLG choose? Justify your recommendation.
questions.model_answer:
National television advertising: TV could build quick awareness of the $640,000 studio across the Melbourne area and show digital tutoring to a mass audience. The drawback is cost and wastage: airtime is expensive for a business with fixed costs of $216,000, a $400,000 loan and a $40,000 overdraft, and most viewers are not parents of the 11,200 course places delivered last quarter, so conversion would be weak and the message poorly targeted.

Partnerships with local schools: NLG already works with local schools, so assemblies, leaflets and parent evenings would reach exactly the families choosing tutoring. This is low-cost, uses the 72% of 400 surveyed parents who would pay $20 more for small-group digital tutoring and the 60% who check pass rates, and builds trust through an existing relationship. It is slower than television and depends on schools allowing access, but it fits NLG's flat structure, where tutors can visit schools directly.

Social media campaigns: Targeted posts can demonstrate the tablet platform and drive sign-ups with measurable clicks against the 5.6-day marker feedback time. They are cheaper than television and reach parents where they already look for reviews, but education purchases rely heavily on trust and pass-rate evidence, so online leads may convert less well than a school-endorsed recommendation.

Recommendation: NLG should choose partnerships with local schools, backed by a modest social media presence for enquiries. This is the cheapest route, uses existing links and matches the 60% who check pass rates. Television is rejected as unaffordable and untargeted for a 55-staff business carrying a $400,000 loan and overdraft; social media alone is rejected because it lacks the credibility that a school partnership provides.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Limited outline of the promotional options with minimal application to NLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Discussion of advantages and disadvantages of at least two options in the context of NLG with some judgement.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed discussion of all three options in the context of NLG with a well-justified recommendation explaining why television and social media are rejected.

questions.question_text: NLG's content error rate has reached 4.1% and tutor absenteeism 9%. Explain two benefits for NLG of using laissez-faire leadership with its workforce of 55.
questions.model_answer:
Point 1: Laissez-faire leadership lets experienced tutors design their own digital materials, which suits NLG's flat structure and can speed up correction of the 4.1% content error rate that rose from 2.3%. Specialists who control their own content can fix errors immediately rather than waiting for approval, protecting the 11,200 course places delivered last quarter and the $28 selling price.

Point 2: Autonomy and trust raise job satisfaction, helping to reduce 9% tutor absenteeism because tutors are not tightly supervised and can arrange their own marking around the 5.6-day feedback time. Lower absence cuts the need to retrain the 18 of 55 tutors missing on-the-job training at $540 each, protecting the return on the $640,000 studio. Flat structures rely on capable people deciding close to the student, so letting tutors shape their own materials fits how NLG already works and shortens the feedback loop when an error appears; the $540 college fee can then be reserved for genuinely new skills.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for each valid benefit identified (max 2).
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NLG's error rate, absenteeism, training and expansion.

questions.question_text: NLG must train 18 of 55 tutors who have not completed on-the-job training on the new learning platform. Consider on-the-job training or off-the-job training at the city college. Which should NLG choose? Justify your decision.
questions.model_answer:
On-the-job training: Coaching on the actual learning platform is directly relevant to NLG's own courses and costs no course fees, while the 18 tutors keep delivering the 11,200 course places from last quarter. Senior tutors can demonstrate how to avoid the 4.1% content error rate immediately. Drawbacks are that busy tutors have less time to teach, local shortcuts may be passed on, and there is no recognised certificate to show the 60% of parents who check pass rates.

Off-the-job training: The city college course at $540 per tutor costs 18 × $540 = $9,720 in total, affordable beside the $640,000 studio. It provides structured digital-pedagogy skills and a recognised certificate that can reassure parents who check pass rates. However, it removes 18 of 55 tutors from the college, which could extend the 5.6-day marker feedback time and worsen 9% absenteeism, and generic content must still be adapted to NLG's own platform.

Decision: NLG should choose on-the-job training first, with a short certified college module later for lead tutors. On-the-job coaching is cheaper, platform-specific and avoids losing teaching capacity while absence is already 9%. Full off-the-job training is rejected now because taking 18 of 55 tutors away would disrupt the 11,200-place schedule and the $9,720 fee is premature before the 4.1% error rate is reduced. Because content errors stand at 4.1%, fixing them while building the real course is more useful than practising on generic examples. NLG should check whether that rate falls for a pilot group and fund the $9,720 college places only if it does not.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Basic description of the two training methods with limited application to NLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Detailed analysis of the benefits and drawbacks of both training methods in the context of NLG.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Comprehensive evaluation of both training methods with a well-justified decision covering cost, disruption and platform relevance.

questions.question_text: Calculate and explain how NLG's management can use its cost, break-even and productivity data.

sub_parts.model_answer: Formula: Break-even output = Fixed costs ÷ Contribution per unit. Substitution: $216,000 ÷ ($28 − $10) = $216,000 ÷ $18 = 12,000 units. Answer: break-even output is 12,000 units a year.
Formula: Contribution per unit = Selling price − Variable cost per unit. Substitution: $28 − $10 = $18. Answer: contribution per unit is $18.

sub_parts.question_text: Explain four ways NLG's management can use this financial data.
sub_parts.model_answer:
1. Comparing the 12,000-unit break-even output with actual output of 50,000 units gives a margin of safety of 38,000 units, showing how far enrolments could fall before the studio makes a loss.
2. Contribution per unit of $18 lets managers test pricing: a $2 discount from $28 to $26 leaves $16 contribution, so they can judge whether extra places still cover the $216,000 fixed costs.
3. Knowing fixed costs and contribution helps set the volume needed to service the $400,000 bank loan and $40,000 overdraft, checking the $640,000 studio can meet repayments.
4. Managers can benchmark unit cost, $216,000 ÷ 50,000 units = $4.32 plus $10 = $14.32 a place, across terms to spot the 4.1% content error rate and 9% tutor absence driving rework.

questions.model_answer: (i) Break-even output = 12,000 units | (ii) Contribution per unit = $18 | (iii) Four contextual uses: 38,000-unit safety margin against 50,000-unit output; discount pricing from $28 against $18 contribution; loan and overdraft servicing for the $640,000 studio; and unit-cost benchmarking at $14.32 to tackle content errors.

working_marks: 1 mark for correct formula/method, 1 mark for accurate numerical answer in (i) and (ii). 1 mark per valid applied point in (iii).

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 2, evaluate NLG's financial performance by calculating the gross profit margin, profit margin and ROCE for 2024 and 2025. Has NLG's financial performance improved? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Calculations:
Gross Profit Margin 2024 = 40.0%
Gross Profit Margin 2025 = 42.0%
Profit Margin 2024 = 15.0%
Profit Margin 2025 = 18.0%
ROCE 2024 = 15.0%
ROCE 2025 = 18.0%

Detailed workings: 2024 gross profit of $720,000 came from $1,800,000 revenue less $1,080,000 cost of sales, so $720,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 40.0. In 2025, $2,250,000 revenue less $1,305,000 cost of sales gives $945,000, so $945,000 ÷ $2,250,000 × 100 = 42.0. Operating profit of $270,000 in 2024 and $405,000 in 2025 divided by revenue gives $270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 and $405,000 ÷ $2,250,000 × 100 = 18.0. Returns on capital were $270,000 ÷ $1,800,000 × 100 = 15.0 in 2024 and $405,000 ÷ $2,250,000 × 100 = 18.0 in 2025. Interest payable rose from $35,000 to $45,000, so the gain was not caused by cheaper borrowing.

Evaluation: All three indicators improved. The gross margin rose from 40.0% to 42.0% because revenue grew from $1,800,000 to $2,250,000 faster than cost of sales, so each course place kept more after direct costs. The operating margin improved from 15.0% to 18.0%, showing the $216,000 fixed-cost base was covered more effectively as the digital studio contributed. Returns on capital climbed from 15.0% to 18.0% even though capital employed rose from $1,800,000 to $2,250,000, so the new investment is already working. These gains are operational because operating profit grew despite higher interest payable. The reservation is the 4.1% content error rate and 9% tutor absence, which could raise rework costs and reverse the trend.

Conclusion: NLG's financial performance has improved. The gross margin (40.0% to 42.0%), operating margin (15.0% to 18.0%) and returns on capital (15.0% to 18.0%) all rose together on higher revenue and gross profit, not on accounting effects. NLG should protect the gain by reducing content errors and absence.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: States financial figures or changes without accurate ratio calculations.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Accurately calculates the three margins/return for both 2024 and 2025 with contextual analysis of the trend.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Accurate calculations for both years with detailed evaluation of revenue, costs, capital and interest movements and a justified conclusion on whether performance improved.

questions.question_text: NLG is considering extending tablet-based courses across all its tutorial colleges. Explain one advantage and one disadvantage for NLG of this decision.
questions.model_answer:
Advantage: Tablet-based courses match the 72% of 400 surveyed parents who would pay $20 more for small-group digital tutoring and the 60% who check pass rates, helping protect the $18 contribution per unit on 50,000 places and supporting the $640,000 studio investment.

Disadvantage: Tablets, licences and support raise the $10 variable cost per unit unless the $20 premium is accepted on every place. The insert gives no figure for the extra technology cost, so the net effect cannot be quantified honestly. Any platform fault would also lift the current 4.1% content error rate and lengthen the 5.6-day marker feedback time before the new studio stabilises. Digital delivery also lets tutors correct the 4.1% content errors faster, supporting the 60% who check pass rates and the studio's reputation with local schools. Since no extra cost figure is given, NLG should trial one cohort and compare rework and complaints before extending the approach to all 55 tutors.

knowledge_max_2: 1 mark for a valid advantage and 1 mark for a valid disadvantage.
application_analysis_max_6: Up to 3 marks per point for detailed contextual development linked to NLG's survey data, costs and quality record.

questions.question_text: Using Appendix 3, evaluate how the base interest rate rise to 4.50%, the 6.2% minimum wage increase to $14.66 and the 8.4% rise in tablet and cloud-licence input costs will affect NLG. Which change will have the greatest impact? Justify your answer.
questions.model_answer:
Interest rate rise (3.75% to 4.50%): The increase is 0.75 of a percentage point, so if NLG's $400,000 ten-year loan is variable-rate the extra cost is 0.75% × $400,000 = $3,000 a year (0.0075 × $400,000). The $40,000 overdraft would also become dearer. That is modest beside fixed costs of $216,000, and a fixed-rate loan would avoid it. Higher rates could make future borrowing dearer and slightly dampen the 5.1% growth in demand for digital tutoring.

Minimum wage increase (6.2%, to $14.66 an hour): NLG's workforce of 55 includes hourly-paid tutor support staff, so payroll costs rise and cannot be avoided. The insert states neither hours worked nor individual pay, so an annual wage total cannot be invented. The defensible test is productivity: 50,000 units ÷ 55 staff = 909.1 places per tutor, so the higher wage is affordable only if that rate holds or improves; cutting 9% absence and the 4.1% error rate and training the 18 untrained tutors can help sustain it.

Input cost inflation (8.4%): Tablets and cloud licences feed the $10 variable cost on every place. The insert does not decompose that cost, so only a bound is honest: if the whole $10 were exposed, 8.4% × $10 = $0.84 per place, and at 50,000 units that is 50,000 × $0.84 = $42,000 a year. Even a smaller exposed share would erode the $18 contribution on every course place sold.

Conclusion: The 8.4% rise in tablet and cloud-licence costs will have the greatest impact. It recurs across all 50,000 places and directly attacks the $18 contribution that services the $400,000 loan and funds the $640,000 studio, whereas the interest rise costs $3,000 a year and the wage effect can be offset by sustaining 909.1 places per tutor. NLG should cut the 4.1% error rate and seek the $20 premium rather than absorb the whole increase.

mark_scheme.level_1_1_to_4: Identifies the external changes with limited application to NLG.
mark_scheme.level_2_5_to_8: Analyses the impact of at least two external changes on NLG's costs, revenue or financing in context.
mark_scheme.level_3_9_to_12: Detailed evaluation of all three changes in context with a well-justified judgment that input-cost inflation has the greatest impact and why the others are smaller.
